content: Recommendation Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all adults living with HIV, regardless of their WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. This recommendation is supported by strong evidence of moderate quality. As a priority, ART should be started in adults with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) or those with a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³. This is also a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. Background Since the initial publication of WHO guidelines on ART in 2002, the evidence base supporting earlier initiation of ART has grown significantly. The 2013 WHO consolidated antiretroviral (ARV) guidelines recommended starting ART in all adults with HIV and a CD4 count ≤500 cells/mm³, regardless of clinical stage. Priority was given to individuals with severe or advanced HIV disease (WHO clinical stages 3 or 4) or a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³. This strong recommendation was based on moderate-quality evidence derived from three randomized controlled trials and 21 observational studies. These studies demonstrated that initiating ART at a CD4 threshold of ≤500 cells/mm³, compared to later initiation, reduced the risk of progression to AIDS, death, tuberculosis (TB), and non-AIDS-defining illnesses, while also improving immune recovery. High-quality evidence from one randomized controlled trial also showed that earlier ART initiation significantly reduced the risk of sexual transmission of HIV to HIV-negative sexual partners in heterosexual couples. Mathematical models and ecological studies further suggested that earlier ART initiation could reduce HIV incidence at the population level, provided there is high uptake of sustained testing, ART coverage, and retention in care. For specific clinical conditions such as TB, hepatitis B virus (HBV) co-infection requiring HBV treatment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, and HIV serodiscordant couples, the 2013 guidelines recommended initiating ART regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. By March 2015, global ART coverage had reached approximately 41% (15 million people). By June 2014, 60% of the 58 WHO HIV focus countries had adopted the CD4 threshold of ≤500 cells/mm³ for ART initiation, and 7% had moved to thresholds above 500 cells/mm³. Despite these advances, the median CD4 count at ART initiation remained significantly below 350 cells/mm³ in most settings, including high-income countries. Late presentation for treatment is associated with high early mortality rates, increased healthcare costs, and poor retention in care. Strengthening the linkage between testing and care, improving health systems to manage patient volumes, and ensuring long-term retention and adherence remain critical challenges. Rationale and Supporting Evidence The recommendation to initiate ART in all adults living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, is supported by evidence and programmatic experience favoring earlier ART initiation. This approach reduces mortality, morbidity, and HIV transmission. Systematic reviews and cohort analyses indicate that untreated HIV infection is associated with the development of several non-AIDS-defining conditions, including cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, liver disease, certain cancers, and neurocognitive disorders. Early ART initiation reduces these events and improves survival. Recent evidence from a large randomized clinical trial demonstrated that ART significantly reduces sexual transmission of HIV among homosexual couples, as previously shown for heterosexual serodiscordant couples. The recommendation to initiate ART at any CD4 count is based on a systematic review with GRADE evidence profiles, which assessed the quality and strength of evidence from one randomized controlled trial and 17 observational studies. These studies reported clinical, immunological, virological, and HIV transmission outcomes. Interim data from the START trial, which was unpublished at the time of the Clinical Guideline Development Group meeting, showed a 57% reduction in negative outcomes (death, AIDS, and serious non-AIDS events) among individuals starting ART immediately compared to those deferring treatment. The trial also demonstrated that immediate ART reduced both AIDS-related and non-AIDS-related events, with the greatest benefit observed for AIDS-related events. These findings were consistent across income levels and geographic regions. Similarly, the HPTN 052 study showed that early ART reduced the risk of HIV sexual transmission to uninfected partners by 93%. This Phase 3 randomized controlled trial enrolled 1,763 HIV serodiscordant couples and followed them for approximately four years. The study found that linked partner infections occurred almost exclusively in the delayed ART group, highlighting the effectiveness of ART in preventing HIV transmission when viral suppression is achieved and maintained. Implementation Considerations Programmatic data from countries offering earlier ART initiation have shown significant increases in ART uptake, reduced time between HIV diagnosis and ART initiation, and higher median CD4 counts at ART initiation. Retention in care has not differed between individuals starting ART at CD4 counts above 500 cells/mm³ and those starting based on standard care thresholds. Research Gaps Further research is needed to evaluate the long-term benefits and potential harms of ART over a lifetime, particularly in settings with high burdens of HIV and TB. Additionally, follow-up studies are required to assess the impact of earlier ART initiation on inflammation-related non-AIDS events and ongoing viral replication. Cost and Cost-Effectiveness Modeling exercises suggest that expanding ART eligibility criteria to include all individuals living with HIV, regardless of CD4 count, could reduce HIV-related mortality by 6–14% over the next decade. The increased cost of earlier ART initiation would be partially offset by reduced hospitalization costs, increased productivity, and prevention of new HIV infections. Simplifying programmatic processes to eliminate the pre-ART period would strengthen the continuum of care and improve outcomes.
